The prince smiled, but did not reply. He was waiting for what she was
going to say next.

“Your elder daughter, Princess Hélène, is a treasure. I don’t know
what could be better. She is so charming, so good, so clever. And your
son, the Count, is so handsome, so distinguished, and so intelligent.
They are both so like you, and yet so different. They are both so
good. I love them both. I am so glad you are coming to the
Englishman’s. I shall be there too. I shall be delighted to see you
all. And I hope you will bring your son-in-law, Prince Bolkónsky. I
have not seen him for a long time. I am told he is very clever. I
should like to make his acquaintance.”

“I will do so with pleasure,” said the prince, and he rose to go.

“Ah, what a pity you are going so soon. I was just going to tell you
about a charming thing that happened to me today. I received a letter

has been to see the Emperor Buonaparte. She is a very clever woman, and
a great favorite of the Empress Josephine. She has written me an
account of the interview. I will read it to you. It is very
interesting.”

“I think that you are unjust, dear friend,” replied the prince. “I
am always thinking of them, and they are always in my heart. But I have
no opportunity of showing them my love. I have no time for them. If I
were a general, or a minister, or a diplomat, I could be with them,
but I am a poor courtier, and I am always occupied with duties I don’t
understand. I am a slave to duty, but I love my children.”

“I don’t believe you. You are always occupied with pleasure, not
with duty. But that is another matter. Your son is at the university,
I think?”

“He has gone to the university. I don’t know if I was right to
allow it; but it is a new fashion, and I may as well let him try it,”
said the prince with a sigh.

“You know, I think, Count, that I am a mother, and I feel interested
in the education of young people. I know, and I am convinced, that
nothing can be compared with the university. It is the best place for
youth. I think that the utmost attention should be paid to the
university. And I am pleased that it is not in Petersburg, but in a
provincial town. There is less dissipation, and it is better for the
character. I was surprised to hear that your son was studying
mathematics. Can he be good at that?”

“Mathematics! He is clever enough, but not for such a career
as that. He is, I think, very clever.”

“Are you not too ambitious for your son? I don’t like the
science of mathematics for young people. I know it is much in fashion
now, but I think it is not a very good thing. It is too cold. I think
medicine would be better, or the law. But the university is excellent
in any case. And I am pleased that he is studying there. And what is
he like? I asked the prince’s wife about him. She is very good, but I
don’t like her. I don’t think she is clever enough for the prince’s
son,” said Anna Pávlovna. “Well, and the poor little princess? How is
she?”

“How do you mean ‘the poor little princess’? She is my treasure,”
said the prince smiling. “I am very pleased that you like her. She
is a very pretty little girl, and very intelligent for her age. She
understands everything. She is fond of music. She has a beautiful voice,
and I am proud of her. She is a great favorite at court. The Emperor
likens her to his sister. He said to me the other day that she had
a very good heart. I think she is very clever. She is a true prince’s
daughter. And she is very fond of me. She is everything to me.”

“Why don’t you take her to the Hermitage? The Emperor would be
so pleased to see her,” said Anna Pávlovna, who, as a court lady,
was always anxious to perform this duty of bringing the prince’s
children to the palace.

“She is still too young. Besides, I am always with her,” said the
prince, who did not like to take his children to the palace, where
he was continually being put to shame by their childishness.

“Ah, that is your fault. It is not right for you to be with her. You
should be at the university, and young people should be brought up by
young people, and not by their father. Why do you not let your son stay
at the university? It is true that he is young and clever, but he is
very young to be there, and he is surely bored by all this. And he has
all the pleasures of Petersburg to tempt him. He is young, and he ought
to be with others of his own age, and not with a father who does not
understand him,” said Anna Pávlovna, who did not like the prince, and
for that reason always wished to find fault with him.

“But I can tell you, Madame, I know why you speak that way. It is
because you have no children of your own. It is easy to find fault with
a father’s affection.”

“No, I am not envious of those who have children. I am not envious
of anyone. But I am sorry for you. I have told you more than once that
the university is a very good thing, and that it is a great pity that
your son does not remain there.”

The prince did not answer.

“Do you know that the countess has been to see me today? I was
quite surprised to see her. She quoted you to me, and I was glad to
hear that you thought it was important to find a suitable match for
Natasha. I think she is a lovely creature, but I don’t think she is
suitable for our society. Few people can be. I think it is very
important that she should have her own circle, and I think that her
marriage with Dolokhov would be very suitable. I know the young man and
I think he is excellent.”

“Dolokhov! Why, he’s a disgrace to society. I don’t understand
how anyone could think of marrying him. I think that he will go to the
university too,” added the prince, in a tone of self-satisfied
knowledge of the subject, but turning away his face from Anna Pávlovna
so as not to contradict her directly.

“Why, he is a young man of family, he is clever, and I don’t know why
you should object to him. You are not at all pleased with the idea of
Natasha’s marriage, and I don’t understand why. The time is coming when
she will have to marry, and I think it would be better for her to marry
now, while she is very young, than later on when she will have to marry
someone much older than herself. I am fond of her, and it would give me
much pleasure to have her married. What are your reasons?”

“I don’t know what reasons.... I am not very much in love with
Dolokhov,” said the prince, yawning.

At that moment the door opened and Dolokhov entered the room.

“Ah, Dolokhov! I was just speaking of you,” said Anna Pávlovna,
with a peculiar smile which did not suit her face, but which was
intended to imply that she was pleased to see him. “I was just
speaking of you and expressing my wish that you should marry the
princess. I think it would be very suitable.”

Dolokhov bowed to the prince and, without looking at Anna Pávlovna,
turned to him and said:

“You know I have just been to see you, but I didn’t find you, so I
came here. I’ve been waiting a long time for your son and had an idea of
coming here.”

“Ah, and you were telling me just now that you wanted to see my
son, and that you had thought of coming here. You are very kind,” said
Anna Pávlovna, smiling at the prince. “Well, you will see him now. He
is here,” said she, addressing Dolokhov.

The prince did not understand why Anna Pávlovna had introduced them,
but he did not like the meeting and turned his back on them.

Prince Vasíli’s son Boris was not yet twenty, but he knew much about
society and was already considered a very good match. He was the son of
a very rich and influential man, a model of the young man of that time.
He had been brought up by the Empress, had been tutor to the royal
children, had been at the university, and was now about to enter the
service and marry. He was a handsome young man, and when he entered the
room with his usual dignified air he was greeted by Dolokhov with
bland deference, as if to show that he did not wish to raise the
subject which was the cause of their meeting, and he was greeted by
Anna Pávlovna with an effusion of friendly warmth. Having heard that
Dolokhov wished to speak to him, he looked uneasily at his father, and
when asked to remain, he sat down with a smile of embarrassment.

Dolokhov, as if to show how indifferent he was to what had taken place
between them, began talking about the English ambassador’s fete,
and Boris, without waiting for him to finish, began talking of the
university and of their former professors, and then they spoke of the
parties at the university, and Dolokhov described some duels, and it
seemed that they were complete strangers and never met before. Boris
talked glibly, but he was distinctly embarrassed, and Dolokhov looked
at him with a peculiar smile, as if he wished to provoke him. Anna
Pávlovna, who was pleased to see the young men, listened to them with
interest, and the prince, who walked about the room, looked at them
with a smile. He liked seeing his son in good society, and the fact
that Dolokhov had come to see his son seemed to him a proof that
Dolokhov intended to make a good marriage. But Anna Pávlovna understood
perfectly that the young men were not talking of the university but of
the duel, and that if Dolokhov had not mentioned it in the room he had
come to seek the prince for the duel, and now that he did not raise the
subject, and seemed to talk of some other matter, it was only in order
not to raise it, and that he did not wish to give offense. She saw that
the prince had not understood this and she was pleased that the young
man was more clever than his father. The prince, who had nothing more
to say, went out of the room. The young men also rose to go, but
Dolokhov, putting his hand on Boris’ shoulder, said he had something to
say to him and sat down again. Boris turned dark red and looked at his
father, who was not yet out of earshot, and said:

“I don’t know what you wish to say to me. I don’t think I can
answer your questions. I have nothing to say to you.”

“But I have something to say to you,” said Dolokhov, looking at
Anna Pávlovna and then at Boris. “I have something to say to you both,”
he added, looking at Boris and then at Anna Pávlovna, and not taking
his eye off her.

“Please come this way,” said Anna Pávlovna, and she went into
another room.

“I want to speak to you, Boris, in private,” said Dolokhov, and
followed Anna Pávlovna.

“What is it?” said Boris, looking angrily at Dolokhov, and
following Anna Pávlovna.

Anna Pávlovna, understanding that they must be left alone, went
into another room. Boris looked at Dolokhov and sat down without
looking at him.

“Boris, I’ve come to ask you about....” Dolokhov began, and
stopping suddenly he looked at Boris with a smile.

“Well, what do you want?” Boris asked irritably. He was afraid of
being left alone with Dolokhov, and he was angry with him for not
having said what he had come to say.

“Well, I’ve come and I’ve said what I came for,” said Dolokhov
smiling. “I’ve come to ask you to arrange a duel between me and your
father.”

Boris turned pale and looked at Dolokhov and at Anna Pávlovna, who
was coming out of the next room, and said, “What!”

“Yes, I’ve come to ask you to arrange a duel between me and your
father. You are the only person I can get this matter settled through,”
said Dolokhov, with a smile.

“Why, the matter is already settled. We are going to fight,” said
Boris, trying to keep a straight face.

“I’ve come to ask you to arrange a duel between me and your
father,” Dolokhov repeated, and smiled.

“Why, how it is that, how it is that, how it is that, I don’t know
how it is, but it is settled. We are going to fight,” said Boris,
laughing, and getting angry.

“Boris, what is it? What’s the matter?” asked Anna Pávlovna,
coming close to them.

“Nothing, nothing, nothing,” answered Boris, and he went out of the
room.


\section*{CHAPTER IV}

“Natasha,” said her mother, “come here, my dear. Prince Vasíli
wishes to speak to you.”

Natasha, who was not at all musical, had been playing the piano and
singing, and was in good spirits. She was in her mother’s room, where
her younger brother, Prince Andrew, was also sitting, reading a book of
his own and gazing intently at the cover. He was an officer, and
wearing a uniform with a star on his breast. He was a tall, slender,
slightly built young man, with a pale and melancholy face, and a short,
iron-gray beard. When he looked up from his book he looked like a
sick man, and almost like a dying man.

Natasha heard her mother’s voice, and was about to go out, but just
then Prince Andrew closed his book and said:

“I’ll go with you, I want to speak to him too.”

“I won’t allow you to speak to him! You know I won’t allow you to
speak to him,” his mother said, looking with a dumb, threatening, and
piteous look at her son.

“Look here, mother, you know he is not a very decent man, and I
can’t sit down and talk to him when I know that he’s such a scoundrel,”
said Prince Andrew.

“Don’t you speak to me like that. I wish to speak with him and not
with you,” said his mother angrily. “I wish to speak with him, and you
are not to interfere.”

Prince Andrew saw that his mother was very angry, and he did not
insist on his point.

“Natasha, we are going to the English ambassador’s,” said his
mother, who did not like him to speak to her in such a tone.

“Yes, I know,” said Natasha, “I’m told we must be at the
ambassador’s at eight.”

“I don’t know what you will do at the ambassador’s, but I will
not go. I don’t want to go,” said his mother. “I’ll stay with
Bolkonski.”

“Very well, mother. We will be back at eleven.”

“Very well, be back at eleven,” said his mother, and Natasha went
with her brother to the door. “It’s a shame that Natasha goes out
to such places, but I can’t help it. He’s the poison. I don’t like
to be alone with him,” thought his mother.

“I’ll go with you,” said Prince Andrew, “if you like, so that
you will not be alone with him,” he added, referring to their father,
who was sitting in the drawing-room.

“No, I don’t want you to go. I prefer to be alone with him,” said
his mother, with a timid smile.

“Oh, very well, we’ll be back at eleven,” said Natasha.

“Don’t be late,” said his mother. “And look after your brother.”

Prince Andrew, who had not wanted to go to the ambassador’s but had
only consented out of respect for his mother, was not in a good mood.
Natasha, when they were alone, went up to him and said:

“Look here, I’m just going to ask him to arrange a duel between
me and Dolokhov.”

All at once Prince Andrew laughed merrily. Natasha was so surprised
that she stopped.

“For goodness’ sake, and what made you say that? I don’t understand
you,” said Prince Andrew.

“Oh, I don’t understand myself. I don’t know. It’s just an idea
that came to me suddenly. I don’t know what made me say it. I don’t
know why I said it. All I know is that I said it and it is so. I don’t
know why. There’s no reason for it. I don’t know. I don’t know,”
said Natasha, laughing and dancing about the room.

“Why, you are mad!” said her brother.

“I don’t know. I don’t know. I don’t know!” she repeated.

“You don’t know? You don’t know?” said Prince Andrew, laughing and
moving about the room with her. “You don’t know? You don’t know?”

“Why, I don’t know.... You don’t know? You don’t know? I don’t
know, but you know,” said Natasha, still laughing.

“No, I don’t know, but you do,” said her brother, also laughing.

“Now I’ll tell you the reason why I said it,” said Natasha,
suddenly ceasing to laugh. “Why did I say it?”

“What did you say?”

“That I was going to ask him to arrange a duel between me and
Dolokhov.”

“It’s not nice for you to say such things to him. Well, what
reason have you for saying it? You know I don’t like Dolokhov.”

“I don’t know. I don’t know. I don’t know. I don’t know. It’s
all nonsense,” said Natasha, sitting down and looking at the floor. “It
is all nonsense. But I’ve said it,” she added, suddenly changing her
look of dejection to one of exultation. “What would you say if I told
you that I was going to marry Dolokhov?”

“Yes, I would say that I cannot understand why it is that you can
say such things to me and that you are not afraid of such things,” said
Prince Andrew.

“I don’t understand it myself. But I shall marry Dolokhov. I’ve
said it. I don’t know what you would say, but I shall marry Dolokhov.”

“But what reason is there? The reason is very clear. You don’t
like him and you don’t like people to say it. And you know that I
don’t like Dolokhov. You know that I don’t like him. Why should you
say such things? You’ve set your heart on it. You have such a way of
doing things! Why do you do it?”

“I don’t know. I don’t know. I don’t know,” said Natasha, as if
laughing at herself. “Don’t ask me, I don’t know why I say anything.
I don’t know why I’ve said it. I don’t know. I don’t know. I don’t
know.”

“Very well. All right,” said Prince Andrew, smiling.

sister for saying that she was going to marry him, and he told her
that she ought not to say things she did not mean. His mother told him
that he had no right to say such things to Natasha, and that it was
very rude and unjust of him. His father said nothing but smiled, and
Anna Pávlovna said nothing, but remembered the young man and decided

pleased because he thought Natasha might help him to get his son the
post in Vienna, and Dolokhov was also pleased because it would be a
good match for him and that the prince would arrange it.

marry him.”

The prince smiled most graciously.

“Let’s talk of your charming elder daughter. I was delighted to
meet your son-in-law. He is charming, really a splendid fellow. You
have married her most happily.”

“It has to be acknowledged that our sovereign sees things with
the eyes of wisdom, and that one must be guided by him in these
matters,” observed the prince. “In the middle of the campaign he
himself, without any of my entreaty, fixed this marriage....”

“Ah, but he is such a fine fellow! Such a delightful companion! I
had no idea that he was so clever. I have already met him twice. We had
an interesting conversation about his travels, and he showed such a
sweet disposition. He spoke at great length of the lady in Dresden he
had seen who bears a striking resemblance to your lovely daughter. The
whole conversation was very pleasant. One could not help noticing that
he is in love with her. I am delighted for her. She has been happy and
is happy, and will be happy. Your son-in-law is such a delightful,
interesting man,” continued Anna Pávlovna, looking pleased and
happy as she spoke of the prince’s eldest son, who had been chosen
by the Empress for her daughter Hélène’s hand. “And now, tell me, do
you know that in Petersburg people are talking of the Princess Bolkonsky
governess? They say she is lovely. What do you think of her?”

“I do not know her.”

“Do you remember when you were staying here last time you said that
this Bolkonsky was a most extraordinary man? And that his character was
so peculiar that he could have no personal ties? that his whole life
was spent in never-ending travels? and that, neglecting all the duties
of a husband and father, he had gone off to the wars again and again?
and that he had quarreled with his wife and forsaken his daughter? and
that his wife was proud and cold and haughty, and his daughter
unmanageable, and that neither he nor they would have anything more to
do with him? They say that this little governess of ours has bewitched
them both and that the Princess, old as she is, has even softened
towards her daughter. And that he, too, has been softening for a year.
The whole family are bewitched by her. I have not seen her, but some
people say she is pretty and fascinating, others say she is not, but she
certainly has something remarkable. What do you think?”

The prince shook his head and smiled with a knowing air. But what
he was really thinking was that he would have liked to go and see this
pretty Frenchwoman, and that he was sorry that it was impossible to do
so without compromising himself.

“I think that the Princess Bolkonsky’s daughter is herself very
pretty,” said the prince, “and could have no need of a governess.”

“Ah, yes, it is true, she has a pretty face and a good figure, but
there is something in her that is disagreeable. She is not well bred
and her manner is strange and repellent. But with the governess she is
charming, and always with her,” said Anna Pávlovna, with a smile
which meant to indicate that she had not made such an investigation
through mere curiosity, but merely for the edification of the prince.

“I think it is a good thing that our young people should come
together,” said the prince. “The Princess Bolkonsky has behaved
very well. She has overcome her pride and... what is she like?”

“We have not yet had the honor of being introduced. She is not a
fascinating woman, but she is very distinguished, and the prince is
exceedingly devoted to her. My husband told me when he came back from
Moscow of their having quarreled, I was sorry for them, the prince is
so good a man, but then I heard that they were now on good terms.”

Anna Pávlovna related this with great animation, and had not
finished when the door was opened and the prince’s daughter, Hélène,
entered the room. The prince rose, took her hand, and with the same
smile which was the chief ornament of his countenance, looked at her.

Hélène, an entirely black-eyed, dark-haired, and fair young woman,
who, like a rose, had in her youthful freshness a hint of the full-blown
blush-rose that was to be, came up to Anna Pávlovna, greeted her
affectionately, and sat down on a chair beside her, which brought her
close to her father. Hélène was very proud of her father and rejoiced
at his presence and his attentions to her. She sat beside Anna Pávlovna
and did not speak, but smiled at her father and at the persons
entering the rooms. Conversation was going on with the men, who were in
the next room, about the English ambassador’s fete. Anna Pávlovna stood
up and Hélène also rose.

“Ah, how lovely you are!” said Anna Pávlovna, looking at her, and
in her voice, her glance, and her smile, all the coquetry of a pretty
woman.

“Who’s here?” said the prince, and lightly kissing his daughter
cheek, he went up to a group of men.

“I tell you what, Anna Pávlovna,” said Hélène, “do you know I
am so pale and thin as to be positively ill? and I have not had a wink
of sleep. The prince is always playing and always dancing and I sit
there in a corner; it’s very tiresome. I am ill.... Really Anna
Pávlovna, please put in a word for me; tell him I am not well, and that
I want to see my father,” said the young woman, her large black eyes
glistening with coquetry.


<a name="page_006"></a:p>

The prince, who was of the same age as Hélène’s father, smiled
in a fatherly way, sat down beside her, and kissing her hand, began to
caress her hair. Hélène was very happy. She rejoiced at her father’s
love, and knew how to take advantage of it.

“Do you know, Anna Pávlovna,” said she, “I am so upset, I hardly
know what I am saying. You see what an old cross I am, I am always ill,”
and she smiled affectionately at her father. “You know, dear father,
when I asked for you I thought you were angry with me.”

“Angry! my dear, I should not dare, I am so happy, I am so delighted,”
said the prince, and always sincere and cordial, he looked into her
eyes, evidently unable to resist the impression of her beauty.

“How happy are you, and yet you have been unlucky, and had a very
tragic affair,” said Anna Pávlovna, who liked to have the prince’s
attention and liked to speak about the tragic event in which he had lost
his wife.

The prince shook his head.

“Why, who can ever speak of that without emotion, and who does not
feel it now!” said he. “I speak of it always with a thrill.”

He looked at his daughter, and, confused, smiled. Anna Pávlovna
knowing how to read the emotions of the heart, understood that the
prince was thinking of the former mistress of his heart—his young and
beautiful wife, who had suddenly been struck down by death—and was
trying to get away from that painful thought by looking at his young and
beautiful daughter, and on seeing his confusion continued to speak of
it.

She told how their late sovereign, when dying, had asked for the
prince to be summoned to his presence, and how he had asked for the
prince’s little daughter, and how the prince, with tears in his eyes,
had kissed the dead hand of the Empress. When she had done speaking the
prince rose, took a cup of tea, and, looking at Hélène, said:

“I must go. I have a word to say to your husband. I purposely
stayed away from his fete yesterday, for I have a word to say to him.
I will be back in a moment.”


<a name="page_007"></a:p>

The prince went away and Anna Pávlovna remained with his daughter,
who, with a smile of intelligence, caught her eye and said:

“He is a delightful man, and I am delighted that I was the cause
of their reconciliation.”

“I am delighted too.”

The prince’s son-in-law, the son of the countess Bezúkhov, the
beautiful old countess, with whom the prince had been in love before he
had brought his wife from Switzerland, was the present Russian
ambassador at Paris, and was one of the most important personages in
the diplomatic world. Bezúkhov was a handsome, fine-looking man, with a
handsome body and a well-groomed head of curling hair, an erect, almost
haughty bearing, and a smile of the highest self-satisfaction. Anna
Pávlovna had been the first to recognize his worth; she had arranged his
marriage with the prince’s eldest daughter, and from the first had done
everything possible to raise him in society. This Bezúkhov was the
prince’s son-in-law, and this diplomatist, well known to all Petersburg,
and one of the most distinguished men in the court world, was Hélène’s
husband. The prince was fond of his daughter and felt proud of this
match for her.

An hour later the prince returned from his son-in-law’s house and
told Anna Pávlovna that his son-in-law had been very kind, and
had promised to write to the Emperor to thank him for his condescension
in transferring the little girl to his own house.

“Tell me, Prince,,” said Anna Pávlovna, “what is the Emperor
like? Is he really so handsome?”

The prince laughed.

“He is young and handsome, as you say,” he replied. “No, he is not
handsome, he is splendid. You are enchanted the moment you see him. He
is like the ideal of a Russian prince. I am sure you will recognize that
at once. Say what you will, the impression is overpowering.

“Oh, how happy we shall be!” said Anna Pávlovna.

“You will see him soon, and then you will judge,” said the prince.

The prince again quoted the Emperor’s words about Hélène’s
daughter. Anna Pávlovna listened attentively and approvingly. She
knew that the prince’s daughter was at that moment at the Emperor’s
court, and it was certainly worth while to make any sacrifice in order
to see her again.

“Ah, if you only knew how happy I am,” said the prince.

At this moment the emigré countess with her daughter entered the
room and greeted Anna Pávlovna and the prince and sat down beside them.

“How well you are looking, my dear countess!” said Anna Pávlovna.
“Tell me, what did you do yesterday?”

“I went to the ball, my good friend,” said the countess simply,
not as if she were answering a question but answering the good wishes
with which her friend met her.

“And how did you like it? Was there anything particular?”

“What can there be, as you know, in a ball?”

“The Emperor, I hear, was surrounded. They say he plays exceedingly
well.”

“I heard him play, yes, indeed, he plays excellently. How
handsome he is, Anna Pávlovna! And you know His Majesty would be
lovely to look at, if he would only cut his long hair. I was delighted
to see the Empress there. I am delighted that everything is so
agreeable. There is such a lively tone in the house! Pardon me, Anna
Pávlovna, for I am tired!”

While the countess was saying that she was tired, she was getting
up, smiling, and putting on her gloves.

“Goodbye, Anna Pávlovna, I am delighted,” and she went out.

War, the emperor, the empress, the court—all that was agreeable
and interesting; but what interested the countess was that the prince
and Anna Pávlovna were talking of what was said about the countess’s
daughter’s beauty and the Emperor’s admiration of it, and that they
were hinting at a possible match between the princess and the Emperor.

The prince and Anna Pávlovna agreed that the princess was very
pretty, and they were speaking of it when the countess entered. She knew
that Anna Pávlovna was repeating what the prince had told her, and she
instantly sensed what they were talking of. She also knew that the
prince was the Emperor’s favorite, and that Anna Pávlovna was
greatly esteemed by her, and as they were talking of what interested
her, she at once joined them and said: “How pretty she is!” and,
accordingly, she was delighted, and said she was tired and went away.
Anna Pávlovna and the prince understood one another so well that in
these five minutes’ conversation with the countess they had spoken
about four things. And yet the countess did not say one word and
appeared not even to take part in the conversation. But in five minutes
she had informed Anna Pávlovna and the prince that the countess
thought the princess very pretty and would like to be acquainted with
her and obtain a place for her at court, and had announced to them that
she herself was tired and was going away. It was most important that she
should say these things, and she had done so. But in saying these
things it was necessary to touch upon other matters which were of no
interest whatever to her, but without which she could not have said
what interested her. And if she had not been able to touch upon such
uninteresting matters it would have been impossible for her to divulge
what interested her. And that was why she spoke of the ball, the
Emperor, the empress, and the prince’s daughter. After she had said
what she had to say, she immediately changed the subject and went away.

Couched in these terms it is all very simple and easy to understand.
But that is not how the countess would have spoken of it. She would
have said that she went into Anna Pávlovna’s rooms, found them full
of people, and after exchanging a few words with them, was tired and
went away. She would certainly not have said that she had gone there
to talk about the princess and her beauty and to make the acquaintance
of the prince and Anna Pávlovna. But in reality that was exactly what
she did.

“Goodbye, Anna Pávlovna, goodbye, Prince! How is the princess? When
will you come?”

These words, so simply uttered, meant: “Thank you, Anna Pávlovna,
for telling the prince that the princess was very pretty, and that the
prince was saying the same thing. Goodbye. I am going to tell the prince
that I think the princess very pretty and I wish to be better
acquainted with her, and that I will intimate to the prince that I am
pleased to have seen you, Anna Pávlovna, and that I regard you as my
friend and am glad to have met you. Prince, I beg you to show me more
attention than you have hitherto. I have come to be acqudnted with you
and Anna Pávlovna. We shall meet again, Anna Pávlovna, and then we can
talk over these things in detail.”

Had the prince known the real meaning of the countess’s words, he
would have been surprised to hear that she esteemed the princess as
pretty. He, who had seen Hélène in her youthful bloom, knew the
beauty of his daughter, and he was surprised that any other woman could
be considered as beautiful as Hélène. He had never seen his son-in-law’s
younger sister. But he knew Anna Pávlovna’s words meant that she
appreciated the princess’s beauty, and he was silent.

“Goodbye, Anna Pávlovna!” said the prince, and he went away.

Anna Pávlovna was a woman of the highest society, a maid of honor,
and for that reason she was transferred from her husband’s house to the
palace. She had intimate relations with the imperial family and with
many people of importance in court circles. She was informed of all
the court intrigues, and these intrigues made up the substance of her
thoughts. Through her friends she knew of the Emperor’s admiration
for the princess. She had alluded to what she knew, and now she was
pleased that the countess had taken up the matter. But Anna Pávlovna
had not the information, the comprehension, or the conviction, and
therefore had no desire to speak of what concerned the princess, for
she felt it was not her affair. But the countess was acquainted with
the princess, and Anna Pávlovna wished to learn more about her.
She wanted the countess to be friendly with her and in that way obtain
all the information she wanted about the princess. But she did not wish
the countess to see that she was interested in the princess, but to
leave her to infer that such was her desire. And therefore she did not
bridge the understanding between them.

“Anna Pávlovna, I am delighted you are with us, and I will come
tomorrow.”

“Anna Pávlovna, how delightful! I am enchanted, Anna Pávlovna,
and I will come in the evening.”

“Anna Pávlovna, I am sure you will be pleased with—,” and the
conversation began. And the countess would immediately have gone away
with this meaning. She would not have spoken of the princess, but
she would have understood that that was what the conversation was
concerned with, and would have gone away, leaving it understood that
she was pleased and that she would come. The countess did not wish to say
that she was pleased and that she would come, but to leave it understood
that she was pleased and would come. So in her conversation the countess
knew of five classes of words: one, words which were spoken for no
purpose (the prince’s daughter, the fete, the ball, etc.). Two, words
which were spoken for the express purpose of giving the impression that
she was pleased and would come. Three, words which were spoken but
which were not understood (Anna Pávlovna, I am delighted, etc.). Four,
words which were spoken and which were understood (I will come, etc.),
and, fifth, the words which were not spoken but which were understood
(what interested her, the countess, and which was the subject of
conversation).

And the countess, and everyone else, talked in this way: first,
selecting certain words from these five classes and saying them with
proper intonation in order to leave it understood that others, which
were not spoken, should be understood. Arranging her words in this way,
the countess understood the prince and Anna Pávlovna’s words and
knew that they were not interested in the fete, the ball, the
prince’s daughter, and the Emperor, but only in the princess whom they
knew to be very pretty.

“Goodbye, Anna Pávlovna!” said the countess, and she went away.

In this story I have not given a single word that was spoken by
the prince and Anna Pávlovna. I have not reproduced their words
because that would have changed the subject. I have related to you
about them only those things that were not actually said, but which you
understand to be the subject of the conversation. The conversation
itself, and what was said, is unimportant and would leave you
uninformed. It is only what is not said, but understood, that is
important and enlightening, for what is not said, but understood, is
what really interests us. Now listen again to what Anna Pávlovna said
to the prince about the princess. Listen and guess what she wished
to convey in those words.

“You know, Prince, did you ever notice that when a woman is very
pretty and clever, she often has a mysterious quality which attracts
and repels a man at the same time? For instance, the Princess Bolkonsky
has that quality. She is an enchanting woman. She never speaks of her
daughter, and it is so natural, but is always so conscious of her
beauty, and knows it so well that at the same time she is proud and
delightful. She is very interesting.”

After listening to these words of Anna Pávlovna’s the prince
naturally asked himself: What is she telling me about? Does she want
me to marry her daughter, or does she want to make a match between the
princess and my son-in-law? Or does she want me to make a match between
her and my son-in-law, or between her and the Countess Bezúkhov? And so
on.

What I have told you is merely an illustration. It is an example
taken from real life, and therefore very complicated. But in this
example you can see clearly how we converse with one another. We say
nothing, but we guess what is understood and take pleasure in it. When
you speak to me, I do not hear what you say, but I hear what is
understood and I am pleased. I am not even interested in what is said
to me, but only in what is understood. When you speak to me you do
not say what you want, but you let me understand it, and I am interested
only in what is understood. And so on.

* * *

After this story we are already in possession of the most important
key to the understanding of all mankind. We have learned to hear not
what is said but to understand what is understood. We have learned to
hear not the words but the meaning. We have learned to hear that which
is not said. And now let us listen to the conversation of two gentlemen.


<a name="page_010"></a:p>

“Eh! What is that? You are a fine one, you are a fine one, indeed, my
young friend. You think yourself something, but a little more, and you
will be in prison. You think you are a good fellow, but I know how
you are.... You think you are a fine fellow, but you are nothing of
the sort. You are a great booby or a great knave, that is all, and your
drilling and brevet colonel is only for the fools. You are nothing of
the sort! You are nothing but a great booby or a great knave.”

“Hullo! I will teach you to insult me, you old fellow!” cried a
fine young man in a new uniform and a new hat, and he seized the old
man by his old, ill-fitting uniform.

“Ah, they are all alike—troublemakers!” The old man with a
grimace of disgust spat at the young man and went away.

“Ungrateful young scoundrel, that’s all! It’s a fine thing to be
young! And I have fought for you, you ungrateful scoundrel. You have
been at the university, and you have studied, and you say I am nothing
but a great booby or a great knave. I have fought for you, I have been
wounded for you, and if you were not a young silly ass, you would
understand that you are indebted to me for the very language you are
speaking in. Yes, I have fought for you. Your father was a serf, and
so was your grandfather. You would have been a serf too if I had not
fought for you, and I have fought for you, and I have been wounded for
you, and I have been ill, and I have endured all kinds of hardships for
you, and for that you call me a great booby or a great knave...”

Here the old man spat again and went away, while the young man
remained standing, staring after him.

Let us guess what these two men said to each other. The old man
called himself all kinds of names and the young man did the same. They
spoke of what they were not interested in at all. But let us guess what
they meant and what they understood. They understood, as you should
have understood in the case of the prince and Anna Pávlovna, since you
have learned to hear what is understood and not what is said.

What did they understand? They understood what the prince and Anna
Pávlovna understood. They understood that they were taking part in a
conversation. In other words, they understood that it was not they who
were taking part in the conversation, and that they did not understand,
nor did they wish to understand, what was being said. They understood
that it was their imitators, who were unknown to them, who were taking
part in the conversation. They understood that what interested them
was not what was being said, but what was understood. They understood
that it was not they, but their imitators, who took offense at what was
being said.

The old man and the young man were only repeating what they had heard
before. They were repeating the words they had heard before, words
which interested them very little but which were understood. They were
talking to each other to pass the time, trying, as people always do,
to show themselves, and to boast to their imitators.

The old man boasted of what he knew, and that was that he had been a
soldier, had suffered, had been wounded, and had been ill, and that he
had fought for the monarchy, and had been honored and rewarded, and
that he was well connected, and that his son was a lieutenant, and that
he was a friend of General Anípkin, who was a colonel, and that he was
interested in a situation in one of the government offices for one of
his friends.

The young man knew that he was the son of a colonel, and that he had
been to the university, and that he belonged to the nobility, and that
he had served, and that he was a lieutenant, and that he had money, and
that he was a good dancer, and that he had studied Latin, and that he
knew French, and that he had been punished, and that he was interested
in a situation for one of his friends. These were the things which the
old man and the young man boasted of and which were understood by
their imitators, who were not they themselves but who were in their
imaginations. Their words, and what they said, were of no interest
to them, for they knew that what was said was not what was understood.
What interested them was not what they said, but what was understood
by their imitators. And they were interested in it not because they
wanted to obtain some advantage for themselves, but because they were
pleased with the result which their words produced.

If the old man had been interested in obtaining a situation for his
friend, he would have asked for it himself, without getting into a
quarrel with the young man. If the young man had been interested in
obtaining a discharge, he would not have insulted the old man. They
were not interested in what they said, but in what was understood by
their imitators, and that was all. But who were these imitators? In
those words both the old man and the young man were imitating themselves
and were therefore taking part in the conversation. They understood
that it was not they who were taking part in the conversation, but their
imitations. They understood that the conversation was being held not
by them, but by their imitators. And that which they were not interested
in, but which was understood, was the opposite of what they said.

The imitator of the old man understood that he was a soldier and
had fought for the monarchy and had been wounded and had been rewarded.
He also understood that he was a friend of General Anípkin, a colonel,
and that he was interested in a situation in a government office.

The imitator of the young man understood that he was the son of a
colonel and that he had been to the university, and had studied Latin,
and knew French, and was a lieutenant, and had served his time, and
had been punished, and was interested in a situation for one of his
friends.

Thus from the very beginning of their conversation the old man
understood that he was not a soldier, and that he had never fought for
the monarchy, and that he had not been wounded and had not been ill,
and that he had never been honored or rewarded, and that he was not a
friend of a colonel, and that he was not interested in a situation for
anyone. The young man understood that he was not a lieutenant, and that
he had not served his time, and that he was not the son of a colonel,
and that he had not been to the university, and had not studied Latin,
and did not know French, and had not been punished.

They understood that what was understood by their imitators was the
opposite of the meaning of their words, and therefore they were pleased
with the result which their conversation produced. And if such is the
result of their conversation, then you will see that it is true that
they understood not what they said but what was understood. And they
understood this because they were not interested in what they said,
but only in what was understood by their imitators. And this
understanding is also interesting, for it is perfectly clear and
unmistakable. What interested the old man was that he was a soldier and
had fought for the monarchy, and had been wounded and had been ill, and
had been honored and rewarded, and that he was a friend of General
Anípkin, and that he was interested in a situation in a government
office. The old man understood that he was not a soldier, and that
he had not fought for the monarchy, and that he had not been wounded
and had not been ill, and that he had not been honored or rewarded, and
that he was not a friend of General Anípkin, and that he was not
interested in a situation in a government office.

Therefore he understood that what was understood by his imitator was
the opposite of what he said. The young man understood all that the
old man understood, for what interested him was that he was the son
of a colonel, and had been to the university, and had studied Latin,
and knew French, and was a lieutenant, and had served his time, and
had been punished, and was interested in a situation for one of his
friends, and that he was angry because the old man called him a
knave. Therefore, the young man understood that he was not the son of
a colonel, and that he had not been to the university, and had not
studied Latin, and did not know French, and was not a lieutenant, and
had not served his time, and had not been punished, and was not
interested in a situation for anyone. And therefore he understood that
what was understood by his imitator was the opposite of what he said.

Since, as you have seen from these two examples, you have learned
to hear what is understood instead of what is said, it will now be
easier for you to understand all mankind, for what is understood is
always clearer, more logical, and more important than what is said. It
is what is understood that interests us. And thus it is evident that
it is always more interesting to hear what is understood than what is
said.

Let us take another example. Listen to what an old lady said to
another lady.

“I am surprised, my dear, that you have not yet seen General
Anípkin. He is a lovely old fellow, you know. A dear, delightful
man, you know. He so took your part, you know, the other day, when you
were having such a dreadful row with your daughter. He was so kind. He
always takes my part, and we old people really must unite to help one
another, and defend the old against the young, you know. They are so
ungrateful! Ah, how I love General Anípkin!”

“I am delighted, my dear, that you have found such a friend. The
old just do not understand the young. It is so delightful to find old
friends, you know, just like in the old days, you know.... And we are
so proud to see that we understand each other. We are so fond of each
other, and we feel so good when we are together, my dear.”

“Ah, and we must help each other, and watch each other’s interests,
and help ourselves, and help the others. We must live for each other,
and we must understand each other, and we must be happy, and help each
other, and watch each other’s interests, and help ourselves, and help
the others.... It is so delightful, my dear, to find such friends as
you and I, you know. I am so happy. Ah! I am delighted.”

“I am delighted, too. But I must go. My daughter has been ill. I
can’t stay. I hope you will forgive me. We must certainly talk
again.”

was understood by their imitators was the opposite of what they said.

The prince listened with a smile, which grew broader the more the
praise of his children grew, and gladly, gladly he liked to hear Anna
Pávlovna speak of his children like that. Yes, they were splendid!

“You have forgotten one of the principal attractions of your evening,”
he said, also smiling. “Miss Hélène Vársuinská will be here. You
know, it’s a very old friendship. She and my Masha are great friends. I
am going to be their chaperon when they go out, so I suppose it is part
of my duty to make Hélène look well.”

“Hélène charms me. She is so witty, I adore her,” said Anna
Pávlovna, though she had once scolded Hélène, who she thought was
rather coarse. “There is one point more you must not forget,” she
added, looking at her watch and thinking of some other little intrigue
that had been begun and was, it seemed, taking some unusual turn.
“There is the new ambassador from Turkey. Seliem Bey is expected at
the fete and he will be introduced here for the first time. A very
important personage—Minister Plenipotentiary and Envoy Extraordinary
of His Highness Abdoul Alem, Sultan of the Ottomans. A man of great
distinction. He has been in Paris and Vienna. What will be reported
about him? Nothing.... No, I beg of you, don’t forget. You must
introduce me to him. And yet I don’t believe in these Turks,” she
added, thinking suddenly of Napoleon and Russia’s position in that
matter. “I don’t believe they are so very great,” she concluded.

“The Sultan Abdoul Alem is a great military power,” said the prince,
but his tone was not certainly the most enthusiastic.

“No, that’s quite another question.”

The prince actually did forget the new ambassador from Turkey, but not
the Vársuinská sisters, and as soon as they arrived with their
chaperon, a lady of advanced age, he hurried up to them.

Anna Pávlovna felt that it was impossible to insist on his
introducing her to the ambassador, for the prince was not studying
current affairs, but was talking to the Vársuinská sisters, so Anna
Pávlovna hastened to take up an offensive position; she knew very well
who was to blame for the new departure in the Turkish policy. Anna
Pávlovna at once began to converse with the new acquaintance, and then
carried out the same manoeuvre with the second man on whom she had set
her sights—the Vicomte de Mortemart. She wanted to secure him for
the Countess Marya Schérer, who was a widow. She took the two men
and thrust them into the midst of the old Duchess Vársuinská and Count
Dolgorúki, two extremely disagreeable old people, and ingratiated
herself with this remarkable couple, and from time to time, not wishing
to be too obvious, had a serious eyeful of the promising pair. Anna
Pávlovna noticed the innuendos at the countess’s expense and the
turns of phrase that in every way favored a mutual understanding of the
problem of the Turkish embassy.

But she was disturbed by something that was taking place in the
corner of the room: the prince was speaking to an unknown young man who
looked like a Frenchman. This young man affected a languid youthfulness
that was not unnatural in him, for he was very young, not yet of age,
and he seemed well suited to the part in which he was cast, and his
manners were more than elegant. Anna Pávlovna did not at all approve of
this connection of the prince’s with this unknown young man, who was
always with him. She did not like their intimacy, and noticed that these
young men were always enemies of each other. She did not like the
existence of this unknown man in the outer world, and would have liked
to know the secret of his connection with the prince.

While this thought passed through her mind, the prince and the young
man moved as if they had been called, and, almost holding each other by
the arm, came over to her. They bowed, and the young man went on to
speak to the duchess and the count, and the prince remained beside Anna
Pávlovna and, smiling, began to speak and explain what they had been
talking about.

At this moment the door opened and Anatole Kurágin, the prince’s
youngest son, entered. He was called the prodigal son of the family,
but there was no need to add the word “prodigal,” for his expenses were
beyond his means. His father was very fond of him, but the prince’s
repeated entreaties that he should economize had failed to produce
any effect on him.

Anatole, as he always entered a room, did not look at anyone, paid
no attention to anyone, but looked at a corner or some object. He
walked across to the green folding doors and stood for some time
forgetting himself, feeling ashamed, and not knowing what to do. Then
recovering himself he nodded to everyone and stood by his father. His
father presented him to Marya Schérer, and that excellent old lady
embraced him, and wished to make a little speech, but from agitation
could manage only one word: “ _Cousin_.”

“Cher cousin,” she said, and Anatole’s lips curved into the most
artificial smile as he always smiled and answered “ _Cher cousin_,”
repeating it, like a pet bird, to all, and embracing the countess like
a blood relation. In the evening Hélène paid him a visit (without her
chaperon; this was not considered necessary) and together they went to a
fete at the French ambassador’s.

The prince had already put his hat on, and, like one accustomed to it,
was mentally preparing himself to go out.

“Mikhail Ilíitch,” he said with a charming smile and turning to the
Vicomte de Mortemart, “je vous prie de proteger celles qui ne vous
protegent pas, _en vous remerciant, en vous remerciant bien._”

The prince departed with the Vársuinská sisters, and before Anna
Pávlovna had time to find a companion for the countess (Mortemart had
been applied to on that account), the young Mortemart was already
asking to be introduced to the “beauté noire”—as he called the
Countess Marya, because she was a brunette and was then wearing mourning
for her husband, who was still not much more than dead.

When the prince and the two sisters had left, Anna Pávlovna saw that
she must again take up the offensive for the Turk. She drew her old
friend the count from the place where he was amusing himself with the
navettes and the Turks, and taking him with her went to an empty corner
where the young Mortemart was deep in conversation with the countess,
and she began to talk to them about the wonders of the Turkish embassy
and the greatness of Abdoul Alem, and at the same moment her eyes
caught sight of an unknown young man who was standing alone in the
corner, in melancholy silence, with his arms folded across his breast
as if reflecting on his life, and his thoughts and the meaning of
existence. His dress was rich and fashionable, but had nothing of the
young man about it. His was not the student dress of the students in
which a young man tries to look like a student, but the dignified and
gentlemanly dress of a well-brought-up, self-possessed, and rich young
man. He was dressed in black velvet, with a gold chain across his white
vest, in the recesses of which one could perceive a shirt of spotless
whiteness. The young man was followed by a man in uniform, his
servant.

This young man was none other than the hero of this story, and was
familiarly called by his family and friends, and by the public, Count
Nikolay Ivánovich Bolkónsky. But the Prince Vasíli, of whom we have
spoken, and with whom he was just then standing, was not acquainted with
him, for Pierre, for all his obvious desire to know something of social
life, had not in those days mixed much among the influential people
of St. Petersburg who frequented Anna Pávlovna’s house, and was
relatively unknown to them.

The prince’s son Anatole was at that moment just finishing the game of
“Navette” with Clara Vársuinská, and getting ready to go to a fete at
the French ambassador’s.

Anatole was a very handsome young man, with a proud erect carriage,
and he talked loudly and cheerfully with Clara Vársuinská, who kept
looking at him with a very pretty smile. The French ambassador had
promised to present them to the wife of the young Turkish ambassador,
the gossip of that day. The ambassador’s wife was as beautiful as her
youth, wealth, and beauty of face were charming, in spite of the
narrow-mindedness to which she succumbed. The Vársuinská sisters were
beaux esprits et les princesses du monde. Their greatest pleasure was
to attach themselves to the distinguished men of the day, who, like the
ambassador of France, had a rendezvous at Anna Pávlovna’s every
evening, and to be presented by them to the most beautiful women in the
highest aristocratic society. And they did not waste all this time for
nothing.

After saluting Marya Schérer, who remained behind, and with Marie they
were conducted by the prince through the hall into the drawing-room.
The two ladies like two radiant suns depicted in an exuberant, richly
decorated and elegant allegory, shone on all sides with their smiles
and demanding nothing but homage. The young lady in an ivory-colored
muslin, with hair shining like green flax and her legs and arms
bare—a blonde, walked in front. Her companion, the brunette Hélène,
a young and fair and noble woman, with brown hair parted in the middle,
and an aureole of curls, had a full white throat, white hands, blue
eyes, and a rosy, bow-shaped mouth: a southern beauty, animated and
animated by the sense of her own power. With her white gloves, white
fingers, and large blue eyes, such as Frenchwomen have, Hélène
reminded one of Cupid and his arrows; in fact she was a lovely
child-woman, all grace and lightness, a young and graceful creature.
She looked with wide-open eyes at the beautiful girls and men who were
passing by, turning her head to look at them.

On reaching the drawing-room the prince and his daughters entered
by the folding doors. When they came in, all the eyes in the room
turned to them, and the low buzzing of voices suddenly became loud and
insistent. All the society ladies with their companions hastened up to
the prince to congratulate him on the great success of his daughters and
to show their interest in the honors they had received. The prince bowed
humbly to them and answered them modestly and even timidly, but in these
words, “My son Anatole is here,” and in the smile he blessed the
society ladies with for their interest in his daughters, a poorly
concealed pride was to be discerned.


. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

In his Kremlin chamber sitting at a large table, the Emperor Alexander
sat at the head of his candle-lit table. He neither spoke nor wrote;
he had been thus sitting for more than an hour, and his attendants, the
overcoat-tailors and the old tailor Kalújnin, who had been set to work
by him to make him a frock-coat, made no sound. The Emperor, with his
broad white hands (hands on which the wrists were the only parts to show
for their ample dimensions) clasped in front of him, and with his head
sunk on his fine-collared white neck, contemplated the half-finished
fitting of this frock-coat and the future state of affairs.

He was furnished with an all too large head, of a childlike beauty; a
massive, straight nose that rose from the high forehead; and with lips,
spiritless and damp, and pale, but with the pudgy seal-like firmness of
a sleeping infant. His hair was streaked with gray, and parted over his
high brow. The Empress was of a gentle disposition and had a tender fond
of her husband, and there was a gentle expression in her eyes and on her
lips harmonizing with her tender name. The Emperor, while grave in his
exterior, was leading a gay life. His chief amusement was the pleasure
of dressing and amusing himself, so he was very fond of his tailor.

The Emperor considered his contending with the “fancy workmen” to make
his frock-coat not too tight or too long, his waistcoat tied in front,
and his round hat not too wide or too deep, a great business of
importance. It taxed all his attention as much as directing an
international expedition. Like a girl who is constrained by her lack of
strength to help to tie her own shoes and is absorbed by such actions,
the Emperor was absorbed in doing things which, though of slight
importance and insignificant at all times, seemed to him important and
interesting because time was left him to think of them. Kalújnin and
the overcoat-tailors folded their elbows and, stamping their feet and
heating their hands, remarked to each other that the Emperor was fat,
and that tails had not yet gone out of fashion. The frock-coat was
finished, and the Emperor, sitting down to lunch, smiled and drew back a
little to see himself in the mirror, and noted that the waistcoat stuck
out too much. The evening was spent at the Alexander Theatre, and in the
evening a dinner-party, with cards and music. The Emperor did not
indulge himself in comic songs, but he danced the waltz, and the
stately _minuet_, his head thrown back, his arms stretched forward and
to the sides, and his legs bent. His favorite occupation was to play at
patience.

The Emperor and Empress had a son, Alexander, who tried to imitate all
his father’s eccentricities in dress and behavior, and in all his
customs, especially his pride in his frock coats.

The Empress Marya Fëdorovna had for a favorite a handsome and
imposing-looking young Frenchman, who was always at her side.


. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

At the time of which we have just been speaking, the last hour in which
the people of St. Petersburg were free and on the eve of a far more
melancholy future, the women of the drawing rooms and salons of the
capital were absorbed in their important affairs and their frolics. The
men did not concern themselves very much about politics, and, except for
the older men, in general were much absorbed in pleasure and in
collaborating with women in the formation of alliances and selections in
society, which seemed essential to them. It was just as in a large
theater at the conclusion of a play, when the actors, the diva and the
heads of the opera, are going through their toilet and preparing for
the long effect of success which the play they have just performed has
made on their behalf. An actor who has played his last part as hero
and a diva who has played her last heroic part are still in their
dressing-rooms, adorned with their jewels and their beautiful costumes,
in the hope of receiving the ovation they have not yet received, and
remind themselves of their former triumphs, while they anxiously await
the new and final applause. It would have been difficult to imagine a
man or a woman in St. Petersburg, in that time of confidence and
communion with the All-powerful Sovereign, who did not believe that she
was living in a great period of the highest importance, and through
which history was passing at the very hour. The year 1805 saw the birth
of Alexander, the realization of the power and authority of Alexander,
the union of the Empress with the great Russian people, the recognition
by the whole civilized world of him, the chosen one, and was the
beginning of the Russian people’s happy connection with the dawn of a
bright future. In the salon of Anna Pávlovna, the son of the great
Rasputin Vársuinská, who, we remember, did not live to see his son,
and who was called “the handsome Rasputin” and “the handsome Prince,”
and the son of Pávlu Yánitsky, who was called “the virtuous Pávlu
Yánitsky,” having gratified their desire for ambition, had at their head
twelve men, chief among whom were Napoleon and Alexander, the superb
and fascinating Rasputin, and the paternal and guru-like Pávlu Yánitsky.
The dark phantoms of the conquered peoples who are always following in
the train of victorious conquerors were not yet as yet in line, but
attendant on the victorious armies in their ranks were the visiting
Turks, the striding ambassadors, and the hovering of the diplomatists.
On men whose repentance for their sins was intending to yoke themselves
to a higher and better life were placing the halo of the new moral
progress, of the “humanitaires.”

The Emperor and the Emperor of France, then holding the cup of victory
in his hand, and holding it with the experience of a fortunate gambler,
counted his winnings. The first and last cry of the young man who sleeps
in the first class of a bed-car, the first call of “Voilá!” was heard,
and as the Emperor of Russia turned and looked into the eyes of the
prince, the waves of his army and the sea of his empire were rolling
under his feet. In the Emperor’s eyes, which had been closed,
everything was illumined by the vision of the liquid, ebbing and
lapping, water-sparkling, golden tinted and silently rolling waves, and
from the depths in his eyes rose the fog. “Trayons” cried his wits,
and confusion and perplexity turned his thoughts to the harmonious and
uniform twilight of the mist around him, and the still, deep, and
uninterrupted murmurs of the army and the empire, and he did not hear
anymore the cries from the carriages or on the platform. What could the
cry of “Voilá!” mean? “I’ve won!” was all that this cry of “Voilá,”
could mean to the Emperor. He was anxious to win. The Empress Marya
Fëdorovna was a devotee. It was she, with her entire family, who was
the first to accept in a thoroughgoing and natural way the superstition
of Russia. She was the first to embrace the idea, on which Napoleon’s
power was founded, as a result of which the battlefields of Russia and
Europe became a Saturnalia of hatred, murder, and despair. No one could
have been a better devotee than the Empress Marya Fëdorovna. Her
superstition was in perfect harmony with her desire for social position,
and with the calibre of her intelligence. The Empress Marya Fëdorovna
was fond of people, and the ladies of her society had, in fact,
established themselves in the very first place in the sovereign’s
affections. The Empress Marya Fëdorovna had also a liking for the
Empress Maria. She was very friendly with the Emperor and Empress Maria,
and especially with the Sissóievskaia, a young lady who was more like
a child than a lady. And she made use of her influence with the Emperor
to secure for this well-beloved lady, who subsisted on the bounty of the
Emperor, the rich gift of a dowry. The women of the royal family were
all together with, and in league against men.

The “male element” was a subject of discussion in the salons of the
women. In the society of the women, the general opinion was that men
were waging a stupid struggle and that they ought to be forced to stop
and give up what they were doing, but the general will and their own
desires prevented them from “giving themselves up.” Neither the women’s
opinion nor the women’s desire prevailed in this matter. The women did
not control men as they did the men of the women, so the women settled
their misunderstandings and differences with each other. The nerve of
thought was strained in the feminine way, with a small nervous effort
through its soft muscles, at the extremity of its fibers; and to the
end of its fibers a more stern and powerful muscle might be applied to
it. The women’s nerves were not strong enough to move that kind of
muscle. The women’s nerves resembled the nerves of a new-born infant
rather than those of a man. The women in themselves, and separately,
were unable to move the sinews of the male nature which drove men on
their terrible and bloody way. Therefore, the women of the salons did
not concern themselves much with thoughts of war, but they followed
with all the force of their feminine souls, with refined and sincere
tenderness, the fate of the woman-children of the Emperor’s circle,
which promised so well. That was the salient point, the beautiful
point, upon which the women’s interests tended to center and concentrate
everything. The women loved, as women do, the women who loved men: they
loved the young Sissóievskaia, the Empress Alexander, and the
princesses, with their bright eyes and tender hearts, intelligent and
capacious minds, singing voices and graceful gestures. They loved them!
With the gentle and earnest entreaty of women, and with the single
purpose of woman for the perfection and superiority of men, the women
formed a choir for the coronation of the devoted women of the Emperor’s
house.
 



                            *CHAPTER III.*


The brilliant fête at the French ambassador’s was not exactly a
soirée, but was intended to be a semi-casual mixture of the usual
soirée and the so-called Russian musical evening and was not on any
account to be a court ball, though, in accordance with the French
ambassador’s habit, much that was usually done at a ball was to be done
here. The incident which had given rise to this fête was the fact that
the wife of the young Turkish ambassador, a woman of extraordinary
prettiness, had been seen at several soirées in the company of the
handsomest young men of the circle of the Russian Court, and talked with
them in French. This evening was to be the last day on which she would
be seen in society until the day on which she would appear as a young
Russian wife.

She was a Circassian girl, a native of Circassia. Her father, having
lost his noble rank, had emigrated to Constantinople with his family. At
one of the Turkish embassies at St. Petersburg a son of the Circassian
prince had been entrusted with a mission at the court of the Emperor
Alexander. This young man was the Turkish ambassador. The fete was
given in honor of his wife, the subject of those conversations, and the
honors of the evening were all accorded to her. The fete was splendid.
Guests came dressed in beautiful evening clothes and diamonds, and the
noble and fine young people of society were there. The room shown to
the guests was magnificently arranged—a long drawing-room with windows
facing the garden. The room was filled, and it was difficult to move
about. The principal guests wore beautiful evening dresses and looked
very handsome. The women were in full dresses with low necks and their
hair loosely waved around their heads. The men wore white frilled
shirts, and their coats had no collars, and were open at the neck. Their
waistcoats were low cut; their watches adorned with beads were gilded
and laid on the shirt above the waist. In the back of each waistcoat,
protruding from the folds of the shirt, there was a bow of ribbon. The
women looked charming in their evening dresses and jewels. Their faces
were like those delicate and precious articles of exquisite workmanship
which are put in a glass case, as if the women thought that the spectators
must be careful not to touch them or strain their necks to look at them.
The men looked more free and easy in their dress and less careful.
There was a good deal of ease and freedom of movement, of the
satisfaction of the senses in their looks. They did not look like,
were not reserved and disdainful, like the women, who seemed to say,
with their eyes wide open, “ _Regardez-moi!_ Look at me. Here I am!
Look at me! Belgium! (or some other jewel) and diamonds! Look if you
like! Mine is better than yours!”

The prince had not yet made his appearance. The ambassador a Dutchman
of German origin, resented the notice of his person. He was a little
thin old gentleman, with a funny moustache, handsome gold spectacles,
and his head bald and shiny. He wore a frieze coat, with his tail up,
and on entering the drawing-room wore a monocle. Just entering, he
was immediately recognized by all as host and master of the fête, and
everyone greeted him with peculiar respect. The ambassador was running
about receiving and greeting the guests. The hostess of the fête, the
Russian ambassador’s wife, a modest and very Frenchwoman in dress and
manners, received each of the principal guests with gracious and
well-bred smiles (“Ah! at last, you here! I am delighted on your
account, I was just gai! Mais, mon Dieu! Am I not tired? It is good! It
is very _fine_! It is fine? In the end, what can you do? Just this, a
piece in your mouth,” etc.), and to each person she spoke two or three
lines of French and Russian. The hostess had a pale and oval face and
light-colored eyes, and a low forehead. Her blonde hair was arranged in
tight curls on the temples and gathered behind. She had recently suffered
an attack of scarlet fever and her face was thin. She was dressed in a
simple and elegant white dress with a narrow sash.

The fete went on. People greeted each other in the French manner (with
the right hand over the heart) and as the Russian ladies came they bowed
a little lower and longer than they ought to have done.

“I beg your indulgence! But I cannot go near the ladies!” How many
times the ladies heard that phrase of the Russian ambassador! When
he said it, he put his hands into his pockets, tilted his head over one
shoulder, and lifted his face toward the women, then, waving his head
toward them, went on to bow. The Russian ambassador spoke French with
incorrect pronunciation. He was tall and thin, with a long, pointed,
protruding chin, and a large forehead above his gaily turned-up eyebrows.
His face looked so severe that guests did not go to him, but went to the
ladies. People now moved about more freely. The host and hostess did not
go up and down the rooms mingling with the guests, but went to them
thems . . .
 

+ + + + + + + + + + + +

“Good! Good! Pourquoi pas?”

“What are you saying, mamma?”

“I was saying that at the death of her husband, the Countess Alexéyevna
had a stroke of apoplexy, which kept her confined to her bed for
several days. One moment, ma caissière! I regret exceedingly that my
snow plows cost more than I had expected. My tax collector has ceased
to give me any trouble, but I must raise the taxes. Ah! How agreeable
that I should have to meet you so very soon after the last time. My
daughter has passed her _maîtrise_ examination. My son has finished
his course. I am going to reward him. I am going to reward him. But
it will take me some time to think of some reward. I think, I will
stay here a little longer and then return home. Another four months!
Impossible! I am glad that I am not staying in this town, for its
inhabitants have all become scarce. The ruler of this town is still
here. I had intended to leave, but I must stay a little longer. I have
now the honor to present to you another Italian who has been taken
ill, likewise afflicted with fever and dysentery. A happy three years!
I am ready to place my services at the disposal of my friends. Indeed,
I am extremely glad that I am not staying in this town, but must stay a
little longer. How happy that I am leaving my home! I am afraid that my
honeymoon will soon be over, and I am proud of having the honor of your
presence in my company; I hope that we may dwell together, and that we
may be together in all weathers. I am afraid, I am much afraid that I
shall not be able to retain my health. I am very glad to have the
pleasure of doing myself the honor of being present at these meetings.
My husband is dead, and I shall never see him again.”

“And why do you speak so much?”

“Because I am getting married!”
